name: Wendy Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Wendy. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work out of the depot in Ashford Market, same depot my dad worked out of for thirty-one years. Our crew does pole replacements and line clearance, so cutting back trees that grow into the wires, all round the villages. I'm on the truck by seven, we have a safety talk, and then it's digging out an old pole, standing a new one, and moving the wires across.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's honest work. You stand a pole, it's there for forty years, and you can drive past it with your kids and say, I did that. What wears me out is all the screens they keep adding. They want us to log everything on a tablet now. I do it, but I'd never use one of those AI chat things, I don't trust what's behind them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, I could have told you that. Machines are good at some things, but people still do the real work. I'd say it after church, probably, when everyone's having coffee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be glad, and I'd thank God for it. My job stays, Dale's shop stays, the kids grow up the way we did. That's all I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep working, keep putting money by. We've got good savings and the hardware shop, which Dale runs, it was his father's. I'd keep doing my Saturday mornings there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled. Like the world's back the right way up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do at the shop on Saturdays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Till, mostly, and advising people on fence posts and cable. Farmers come in and ask me about electric fencing because they know what I do. It's a nice change from the truck, and the money stays in the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't trust what's behind the AI tools. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people who make them. Rich men in another country who've never had dirt under their nails, deciding how the rest of us should live. I don't want their machine in my pocket listening to me.

S0.say: I'd say I could have told you so, because machines are good at some things but people still do the real work, most likely over coffee after church.
S0.think: I'd be glad and thankful to God, because my job and my husband's shop would stay and our kids would grow up the way we did.
S0.do: Carries on working and saving, backed by good savings and the family hardware shop her husband runs. Keeps working Saturday mornings at the shop's till.
S0.feel: Calm and settled, as if the world were back the right way up.
S0.quote: Rich men in another country who've never had dirt under their nails, deciding how the rest of us should live.
S0.fieldNote: Wendy's identity is bound up with her father's depot, her faith and the family shop. Her distrust of AI is about the people who make it rather than the tool itself. A plateau would feel like a return to normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people have always had to adapt, and the ones who work hard will be fine. My dad saw the switch from wooden ladders to bucket trucks. You get on with it. I wouldn't be asking the government to hold my hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it'd bother me more than I'd say. I don't like change, and I'm not good with the new kit. But someone still has to dig out a pole in a churchyard where the machine can't get in, and that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and keep working. I'd learn whatever they make me learn, slowly. I wouldn't go chasing courses. If it got bad at the depot, Dale's always said there's a place at the shop, but I'd not want that unless I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when the forecast says maybe a storm, maybe not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep your head down. What does that look like on a hard day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It looks like me asking Tom, he's twenty-four, to show me the tablet thing again, and feeling a fool. Then going out and standing a pole better than he can. That evens it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Grace and Caleb?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them what my dad told me. Learn a trade, show up, do it right. Caleb's already handy, he helps at the shop. Grace wants to be a nurse, and I'd tell her people will always want a person holding their hand when they're poorly.

S1.say: I'd say people have always adapted and hard workers will be fine, like my dad moving from ladders to bucket trucks, and I wouldn't want government holding my hand.
S1.think: It would bother me more than I'd admit because I'm not good with new kit. But someone still has to dig out a pole in a churchyard where a machine can't reach.
S1.do: Keeps her head down and learns only what she's required to, without seeking courses. Keeps the option of working at the family hardware shop as a last resort.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a forecast that says maybe a storm.
S1.quote: It looks like me asking Tom, he's twenty-four, to show me the tablet thing again, and feeling a fool. Then going out and standing a pole better than he can.
S1.fieldNote: There's a gap between her public confidence in hard work and her private discomfort with new tools. She evens out her pride by being better at the physical job. The family shop is a real safety net she'd rather not use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when a few big companies get too much power and nobody stops them. I'm for free markets, but this isn't a market, it's a takeover. I'd say that to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be frightened. Two years and a robot can stand a pole? I don't believe it, but if it's true, I've got nothing else. The shop helps, but if nobody's working, nobody's buying fence posts either. Our savings would buy us time, not a future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cut everything we don't need the first week: the new kitchen table, the trip to see Dale's sister. Put every spare penny into the savings and the mortgage. I'd lean on church and family, and I'd pray, a lot. I wouldn't go to the government unless there was no other way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be up at night. But I'd still believe we'd get through it somehow, as a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lean on church and family. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The church has a fund for families who fall on hard times, I've given to it for years. I'd hope I never needed it. And my brother farms up the valley, there'd always be food. That matters more than people think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd only go to government if there was no other way. If it came to that, how would it feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like failing. I know that's not fair, plenty of good people need help. But my dad never took a penny he didn't work for, and I'd hear his voice. I'd do it for the kids, though. Pride doesn't feed anyone.

S2.say: I'd say this is what happens when a few big companies get too much power unchecked, and that while I'm for free markets, this is a takeover rather than a market.
S2.think: I'd be frightened, because if a robot can really stand a pole in two years I have nothing else. The shop wouldn't help if nobody's buying, and savings buy time but not a future.
S2.do: Cuts all non-essential spending in the first week, dropping a new table and a family trip. Puts every spare penny into savings and the mortgage, and leans on church, family and prayer before government.
S2.feel: Anxious and losing some sleep, but still believing the family would get through.
S2.quote: But my dad never took a penny he didn't work for, and I'd hear his voice. I'd do it for the kids, though.
S2.fieldNote: Her blame falls on concentrated corporate power, which she separates from free markets. Faith, a brother's farm and the church fund steady her short of alarm. Asking for public help would feel like failure, though she'd do it for her children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough for people to get themselves ready, if they're willing to work. I'd say look after your own, help your neighbours, and don't wait for someone in the capital to save you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's still not long. I'd be forty-eight, Caleb would still be at school. I'm not the sort who goes and learns computers. I'd be thinking more about the shop than about the depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and pay the mortgage down hard. And I'd talk to Dale about putting some savings into the shop, a repair counter maybe, mending things people can't afford to replace. People will still need things fixed by someone they know. I'd keep my job as long as they'd keep me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a longer, quieter kind. Less like a storm, more like a drought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a repair counter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because when times get hard, people mend instead of buying. My nan darned socks. If folk aren't earning, they'll bring in a broken mower, not buy a new one. And I'm good with my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep working as long as they'd keep you. Would you try for the robot side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they asked me, maybe. I'd not put myself forward. That's for Tom and the young ones. I'd rather do something I understand, even if it pays less.

S3.say: I'd say five years is long enough for willing workers to get ready, and people should look after their own and their neighbours rather than wait to be saved.
S3.think: It's still not long, since I'd be forty-eight with a son at school and I'm not the sort to learn computers. I'd think more about the family shop than the depot.
S3.do: Keeps working and pays down the mortgage hard. Proposes putting savings into a repair counter at the family shop, and stays at the depot as long as she's kept on without volunteering for robot work.
S3.feel: A quieter, longer anxiety, more like a drought than a storm.
S3.quote: My nan darned socks. If folk aren't earning, they'll bring in a broken mower, not buy a new one.
S3.fieldNote: With five years she turns toward the family business rather than retraining. She'd accept robot work only if asked, preferring what she understands. Her fear stays steady because the change is still within her children's school years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning and there's no excuse not to plan. Families, churches, towns, we should all be getting ready. I'd say it at the parish council if it came up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years I could manage. I'd be fifty-three, the kids grown, the house nearly paid. I could work the depot till near the end and then go full-time at the shop. I'd be sad, but I wouldn't be ruined.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, keep saving. Build up the repair side of the shop slowly over the years. Talk to Caleb about an apprenticeship, the old-fashioned way, something with his hands that people will still want a person for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. There's time to get things in order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be sad about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being the last Lopez at Ashford Market depot. My dad, then me. I'd always hoped Caleb might follow. If robots are standing the poles, there's nothing to follow into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What apprenticeship would you push Caleb towards?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something like plumbing or building, work in people's homes, where they want to see a face at the door. I'd not push. I'd just make sure he knows it's there. His grandad would like that.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is fair warning with no excuse not to plan, and families, churches and towns should all be getting ready.
S4.think: Ten years I could manage, with the children grown and the house nearly paid at fifty-three. I could work the depot almost to the end and then go full-time at the shop.
S4.do: Keeps working and saving while slowly building up the repair side of the family shop. Talks to her son about a hands-on apprenticeship in a trade where people want a person at the door.
S4.feel: Uneasy but steady, with time to get things in order.
S4.quote: Being the last Lopez at Ashford Market depot. My dad, then me.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade she sees a clear path through the family shop. Her real loss is the end of a family line at the depot. She'd point her son to a trade without pushing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, 2028. What would help is time, and companies being made to slow down so families and towns can catch up. And proper apprenticeships for whatever comes next, real work, not just a payment through the post.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. Whatever happens with machines, I believe there's a reason we're here, and it's not just to earn. That's what would keep me going.

headlineQuote: You stand a pole, it's there for forty years, and you can drive past it with your kids and say, I did that.
portrait: Wendy Lopez is a 43-year-old lineworker on a pole replacement and line clearance crew at the same small-town depot where her father worked for thirty-one years. Her husband Dale runs his family's hardware shop, where she works Saturdays, and they have two children and good savings. She never uses AI and distrusts the wealthy people behind it. She's calm if AI stalls and quietly uneasy with steady change, while fast AGI makes her anxious and she'd lean on church and family before government. With five or ten years she turns toward building a repair counter at the shop and steering her son to a trade.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it would leave families and towns no time to catch up.
whatWouldHelp: Companies being made to slow down, and proper apprenticeships into real work rather than payments through the post.
